blocks.text: But Scaliger, in his Exercise 231 against Cardano, taught me another proof of στοργῆς [storgēs] in the vulture, in these words: They say that the African vulture in Libya and on Mount Atlas, where they call it sner, lives so long that, stripped of its feathers, it is fed by its own young; so that the Greeks must now coin another word than ἀντιπελαργεῖν [antipelargein], namely ἀντοιωνεῖν [antoiōnein]. Since these words harm no one, I do not understand why they so stirred that cymbal of the world, Leo Allatius, that he took from them material for raging without restraint against a man by far the greatest, in his Notes on Eustathius' Hexaemeron, p. 225. Most wittily, he says, he jests at the Greeks, as if on the strength of this story they must coin another name than ἀντιπελαργεῖν [antipelargein], namely ἀντοιωνεῖν [antoiōnein]. Yet so great a man, corrector and propagator of the Greek and Latin languages, ἀποῤῥοιβδεῖ [aporrhoibdei], καὶ τοῖς ἐκ τρίποδος βδέει λιβανωτοὺς [kai tois ek tripodos bdeei libanōtous], and fancies that he smells sweet. The name the Greeks are to coin ought to be taken from the vulture, whose nature and character are to be expressed, not from birds, most of whom [quorum plerique] are found to be undutiful to their parents. In this, note the words quorum (of birds) plerique impii. For Scaliger's critic did not know that aves [birds] is of feminine gender, which boys learn under the cane. But these are trifles compared with what follows: But to Scaliger everything sounds as it pleases him, and so does this. And Scaliger coins it thus, but a Greek does not; if he wished to form it from the vulture, he would certainly not say, in correct form, ἀντιγυπίζειν [antigypizein]. And a little later, as though he had done the job well: Behold (he says) the smatterers of Greeklings whom you unjustly tear apart against all right! Such as they are, they nevertheless recognize both your ignorance and your trifles. Sell smoke to others; they possess the light. As if he tears apart the Greeks who writes that they must now say ἀντοιωνεῖν [antoiōnein] of the vulture, as ἀντιπελαργεῖν [antipelargein] of the stork. For that is all that Scaliger wrote. So there was no reason for him to stir up such tragedies. Nor should it have escaped a Greek that many centuries ago οἰωνὸν [oiōnon] was rendered γῦπα [gypa] by most Grammarians. The Etymologicum magnum: Οἰωνός· ὄρνις, ὁ γύψ· παρὰ τοῦ οἰῶ τὸ μονῶ γίνεται. Φασὶ γάρ τινες, ὅτι καὶ χωρὶς μίξεως πέφυκε πολλάκις τίκτειν [Oiōnos; ornis, ho gyps; para tou oiō to monō ginetai. Phasi gar tines, hoti kai chōris mixeōs pephyke pollakis tiktein], etc. The unpublished Lexicon of Cyril, which I have in my possession: Οἰωνός· ὁ γὺψ [Oiōnos; ho gyps], etc., almost as [III, 77] in the Etymologicum. The Scholiast of Sophocles on the Ajax, line 842: Οἰωνοῖς· ὄρνισιν· κυρίως δὲ οἱ γῦπες [Oiōnois; ornisin; kyriōs de hoi gypes]. Oppian's Scholiast on line 29 of book 1 of the Halieutica: Οἰωνοί· τὰ ὄρνεα, κυρίως δὲ οἱ γῦπες, ἀπὸ τοῦ οἰῶ τὸ μονῶ. Μεμονωμένον γὰρ συλλαμβάνει ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀνέμου, μὴ ὄντος ἄῤῥενος [Oiōnoi; ta ornea, kyriōs de hoi gypes, apo tou oiō to monō. Memonōmenon gar syllambanei hypo tou anemou, mē ontos arrhenos]. Io. Tzetzes on Hesiod's Works and Days: Οἰωνοὶ κυρίως οἱ γῦπες, ὡς οἰοὶ, ἤτοι μόνοι, δίχα συνουσίας, ὠὰ ὑπηνέμια γεννῶντες [Oiōnoi kyriōs hoi gypes, hōs oioi, ētoi monoi, dicha synousias, ōa hypēnemia gennōntes]. And in Chiliad 13, History 474:

Γῦπες κυρίως οἰωνοί. θῆλυ γὰρ πᾶν τὸ γένος. Οἶαι, καὶ μόναι, κύουσαι ὠὰ, μηδ᾽ ἐξ ἀῤῥένων. Ὠὰ γὰρ ὑπηνέμια γεννῶσιν, ὡς προεῖπον. Οὕτω κυρίως οἰωνοὶ καλοῦνται μὲν οἱ γῦπες. Καὶ πάντα δὲ τὰ ὄρνεα καταχρηστικωτέρως. [Gypes kyriōs oiōnoi. thēly gar pan to genos. Oiai, kai monai, kyousai ōa, mēd᾽ ex arrhenōn. Ōa gar hypēnemia gennōsin, hōs proeipon. Houtō kyriōs oiōnoi kalountai men hoi gypes. Kai panta de ta ornea katachrēstikōterōs.]

If you knew this, my Allatius, with what face did you charge Scaliger with ignorance, when he assumed as true what the most learned of your countrymen assert so plainly and with such unanimous agreement? Or, if you did not know it, since you are ignorant of things most hackneyed and on everyone's lips, with what face did you dare to match yourself against such a man, not fearing that the well-known line would be thrown at you,
Νεκροῦ σῶμα λέοντος ἐφυβρίζουσι λαγωοί. [Nekrou sōma leontos ephybrizousi lagōoi.]
Meanwhile I admit what no one is unaware of, that οἰωνὸν [oiōnon] is often taken for any bird, especially if it is rapacious or carnivorous: as at the very beginning of the Iliad,

that is, τοῖς σαρκοφάγοις ὄρνισι [tois sarkophagois ornisi], especially γυψὶ, καὶ κόραξιν [gypsi, kai koraxin], as the old Scholiast has it there. Hence Hesychius: Οἰωνοί· σαρκοφάγα ὄρνεα, καὶ πάντα, γῦπες, κόρακες [Oiōnoi; sarkophaga ornea, kai panta, gypes, korakes]. But this too is very well known, that the name of a genus is often restricted to a species. Thus ὄρνις [ornis], bird, is often the hen. Θὴρ [Thēr], wild beast, is often the lion. Θηρία [Thēria], wild beasts, are often serpents, or even vipers, whence Θηριακά [Thēriaka]. Ὑποζύγιον [Hypozygion], beast of burden, is used everywhere by the Greek translators for the ass, and following them by Matthew, Peter, etc. For us jumentum is a mare. For you today ἄλογον [alogon] is a horse, which seems already to have prevailed in the age of Hesychius, whose words are: Καπητόν· παράβλημα ἀλόγων [Kapēton; parablēma alogōn]; for which I would read Κάπη· τὸ παράβλημα ἀλόγων [Kapē; to parablēma alogōn], that is, fodder of horses. Since Κάπη [Kapē] commonly means a horses' manger, Hesychius had found it used somewhere for the fodder usually put before horses in the manger.
